summary: Defines OSPFv2 routing extensions that meet the requirements for routing in an Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON), as described by the ITU-T, on top of GMPLS. It was an experimental specification and has been replaced by RFC 6827.

eli5.summary: Cables of light carry traffic between cities, and this adds rules so the signposts can describe those light paths too. It was later replaced by a newer version.

subtitle: Extending OSPF routing to control optical transport networks.

tldr.problem: Optical networks carry vast amounts of traffic between cities and data centers, but standard routing protocols like OSPF were designed before optical switching became practical. The ITU-T's ASON architecture defines how to control optical networks, but OSPF needs extensions to advertise optical network resources and manage hierarchical routing areas.
tldr.mechanism: This specification extends OSPFv2 with new fields to advertise reachable IP addresses on each node, support for multiple logical control plane entities per router, hierarchical routing area management, and mechanisms for information to flow up and down the hierarchy without looping.
tldr.outcome: Optical transport networks can now be controlled using GMPLS with OSPF as the routing protocol, allowing operators to use ASON's layered, hierarchical approach. It was replaced by RFC 6827 with updated definitions.

today: RFC 6827 obsoleted this specification, providing updated OSPF extensions for ASON routing with revised definitions. This RFC is Experimental and has been superseded.

sections.title: ASON and Optical Network Routing
sections.content:
Fiber optic cables form the backbone of the Internet, carrying traffic between continents and data centers at enormous speeds. The Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) is an architecture defined by the ITU-T that applies control-plane automation to optical networks—allowing them to set up, tear down, and reroute light paths automatically, similar to how traditional packet networks work.

GMPLS (Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching) is the control-plane protocol suite used to control ASON. It extends MPLS concepts from packet networks to optical networks, where connections are set up using wavelengths, time slots, or fiber channels.

OSPF is the most widely used routing protocol in the Internet. This specification extends OSPF to meet the routing requirements of ASON as described in RFC 4258. The extensions allow OSPF to advertise optical resources, support hierarchical organization of routing areas, and manage how routing information flows between levels of the hierarchy.
sections.eli5: Big fiber cables can now automatically switch paths like a smart network, and OSPF is the signpost system that tells them where to send light. This upgrade lets OSPF understand the special rules that fiber networks use.

sections.title: Routing Areas, Hierarchy, and Protocol Instances
sections.content:
In ASON, a routing area (RA) represents a partition of the data plane—a region of the optical network. Multiple RAs can be arranged hierarchically: a larger RA can contain smaller RAs connected by links, forming a tree-like structure.

OSPF already has areas, but the hierarchy of ASON RAs does not map one-to-one to OSPF areas. Instead, each level of the RA hierarchy is represented by a separate instance of the OSPF protocol. A router can run multiple OSPF instances, each managing a different level of the hierarchy. This allows routing information to be exchanged between levels using import/export rules rather than the traditional OSPF inter-area mechanism.

A single OSPF instance plus a specific OSPF area together identify an ASON routing area. This allows operators to use configuration and naming that keeps the ASON hierarchy explicit and manageable.
sections.eli5: Optical networks have layers like a stack of trays. Each layer has its own OSPF signpost system that talks to the layer above and below using special rules, not by traditional area connections.

sections.title: Advertising Reachable Addresses and Network Prefixes
sections.content:
In a complex optical network with multiple logical control-plane entities, it is important to advertise which IP addresses are reachable on each node. The specification defines new sub-TLVs (Type-Length-Value fields) for this purpose.

A Node IPv4 Local Prefix sub-TLV advertises one or more IPv4 address prefixes that are local to a node. Each prefix is paired with a network mask. Similarly, the Node IPv6 Local Prefix sub-TLV advertises IPv6 prefixes. These sub-TLVs are carried in the Node Attribute TLV of OSPF's opaque TE (traffic engineering) LSAs.

When a router in the control plane represents multiple logical TE routers (nodes on the data plane), a separate sub-TLV associates local prefixes with a specific TE Router ID. This allows the control plane to disambiguate which addresses belong to which data-plane node.

The local addresses already visible in the TE LSAs (such as router addresses and interface addresses) should not be redundantly advertised in these new sub-TLVs, to avoid clutter in the routing database.
sections.eli5: Each fiber node announces which phone numbers (IP addresses) it can reach. The system uses special labels so it's clear which addresses belong to which fiber node in a complex setup.

sections.title: Routing Information Flow and Import/Export Rules
sections.content:
In a hierarchical ASON network, routing information must flow both upward (from lower levels toward the top) and downward (from higher levels to lower). The specification defines rules for importing and exporting routing information between OSPF instances.

Routing information is exchanged as opaque TE LSAs. An import/export rule prevents a piece of routing information from being imported back into the OSPF area from which it came. This avoids loops and unnecessary duplication. Information may also be filtered or aggregated as it moves between levels, according to local policy.

A routing controller (RC) in one RA can import routing information from adjacent levels and re-originate it with its own Router ID. The specification defines two capability bits: the U bit indicates the router can export information upward, and the D bit indicates it can export downward. When multiple RCs are present, the one with the highest Router ID is selected for each direction, providing a simple and robust selection mechanism.

The specification also defines a Router Information Experimental Capabilities TLV to carry these flags in the Router Information LSA, allowing RCs to discover each other and select leaders for information dissemination.
sections.eli5: Information flows up and down the layers, but there are rules to prevent it from going in circles. The system picks one main router at each level to send information up and another to send information down.

sections.title: Link Advertisement and Multi-Node Router Representations
sections.content:
In ASON, a single control-plane router may represent multiple data-plane nodes (each with its own TE Router ID). To disambiguate which links and addresses belong to which data-plane node, new sub-TLVs are introduced.

A Local and Remote TE Router ID sub-TLV explicitly identifies both the local and remote TE Router IDs at the ends of a link. This is necessary when a single Router ID (control-plane entity) advertises links on behalf of multiple TE Router IDs (data-plane nodes). The sub-TLV carries both identifiers, allowing downstream routers to correctly associate the link with the right data-plane entities.

These sub-TLVs are included only when necessary (when a Router ID represents more than one TE Router ID), to keep the routing database lean. The same principle applies to reachability information: when multiple TE Router IDs are involved, explicit association sub-TLVs prevent confusion about which addresses are reachable via which data-plane node.

The specification also discusses bandwidth accounting: GMPLS already carries bandwidth and switching-capability information per interface. The specification notes that technology-specific information may be defined separately in other documents, but does not extend bandwidth fields here.
sections.eli5: When one control signpost represents many fiber nodes, it uses special tags to make clear which links and addresses belong to which one. This prevents mix-ups in the routing database.
